analogy.p: Imagine rolling out a sheet of dough and cutting round biscuits. The mass of the dough is your reactants; the biscuits are the **desired product**; the leftover scraps between the circles are the **by-product**. If the biscuits only make up 56% of the dough's mass, then the atom economy is 56%, however carefully you bake them. A cutter that uses nearly all the dough is a high atom economy reaction. This analogy fails because the left-over dough can simply be re-rolled, whereas in a chemical reaction the unwanted atoms are fixed into a different substance and cannot be reused unless a new reaction is run.

bullets: **Atom economy** = the proportion (percentage) of the mass of the reactants that becomes the desired product, in theory.
It is calculated from the **balanced equation**, so you do not need any experimental data.
A reaction that makes **only one product** (such as an addition reaction) has an atom economy of **100%**.
A reaction that makes a desired product plus by-products has an atom economy **below 100%**.
It tells you how much of the starting material is **wasted as by-products** even if the percentage yield is 100%.
Atom economy is a key idea in **green chemistry** and sustainable development.
core.p: The **atom economy** of a reaction is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. In every reaction the total mass is conserved, but if the equation makes the wanted product plus one or more other products, then some of the reactant mass ends up as waste. A reaction with a high atom economy turns most of the reactant atoms into the wanted product, so little is wasted. It is worked out from the balanced equation only, so it is a property of the reaction, not of how well you carried out the experiment.

bullets: **Atom economy (%) = (relative formula mass of desired product from the equation ÷ sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation) × 100**
Multiply each Mr by its **coefficient** (big number) in the balanced equation before adding.
Use **only the desired product** on the top line, not the by-products.
The sum of the reactants' Mr values equals the sum of the products' Mr values (conservation of mass).
The answer is a percentage between 0% and 100% and has no other unit.
Use the Ar values from the Periodic Table, for example Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16, Fe = 56, Al = 27.
core.p: The calculation compares the relative formula mass (Mr) of the wanted product with the total Mr of all the reactants, using the numbers of moles shown in the balanced equation. Where there is a big number in front of a formula you must multiply its Mr by that number. As a check, the total Mr of the reactants should equal the total Mr of the products, because mass is conserved.

bullets: Step 1: write the **balanced symbol equation** (check atoms on both sides).
Step 2: work out the **Mr of each substance** from the Periodic Table.
Step 3: multiply each Mr by its **coefficient** (number of moles in the equation).
Step 4: add the masses of **all reactants** to get the total.
Step 5: identify the **desired product** and its total mass from the equation.
Step 6: **divide desired product mass by total reactant mass and multiply by 100**.
core.h: Calculating atom economy step by step
core.p: Always follow a clear structure to gain method marks: balance the equation, work out each Mr, multiply by the coefficients, add up the reactants, pick out the desired product, and divide. Setting your working out in lines makes errors easy to spot. The examples later in these notes use calcium carbonate, iron(III) oxide and aluminium oxide so you can practise with real exam reactions.

bullets: Mr CaO = 40 + 16 = **56**; Mr CO2 = 12 + 32 = **44**; and 56 + 44 = 100, which confirms conservation of mass.
Atom economy for CaO = 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = **56%**.
If the CO2 were the desired product the atom economy would be **44%**, so the answer depends on which product is wanted.
A **single reactant splitting into two products** will always be below 100% for either product.
Capturing and using the CO2 (for example for fizzy drinks) would make use of the by-product.
core.p: In the thermal decomposition CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 the useful product is calcium oxide (quicklime) used to make cement and to neutralise soil. The carbon dioxide is a by-product. The Mr of CaCO3 is 40 + 12 + 48 = 100, and the Mr of CaO is 56. So the atom economy is 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56%, which means 44% of the mass of the reactant becomes carbon dioxide. Decompositions always have a low atom economy for the wanted solid because a gas is given off.

bullets: Mr Fe2O3 = **160**; Mr CO = **28**, and the equation uses **3CO**, so 3 × 28 = **84**.
Total reactants = 160 + 84 = **244**.
Desired product: 2Fe = 2 × 56 = **112**.
The low atom economy shows why recycling metals avoids this waste.
core.h: Worked reaction type 2: reduction of a metal ore
core.p: Metals are often extracted by reducing their oxides. For iron: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. The Mr of Fe2O3 is (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160 and three moles of CO gives 3 × 28 = 84, so the total is 244. The iron made is 2 × 56 = 112, so the atom economy is 112 ÷ 244 × 100 = 45.9%. More than half the reactant mass ends up as carbon dioxide, which shows why metal extraction processes have low atom economy.

bullets: Desired product: 4Al = 4 × 27 = **108**.
Remember to use the **balanced** equation: the doubled coefficients change the answer if you forget them.
The oxygen could be sold, but in practice it reacts with the hot carbon anodes.
core.h: Worked reaction type 3: electrolysis of aluminium oxide
core.p: The extraction of aluminium follows 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2. The Mr of Al2O3 is (2 × 27) + (3 × 16) = 102, and two moles give 204. The desired product is 4 × 27 = 108 g of aluminium. The atom economy is 108 ÷ 204 × 100 = 52.9%. The oxygen is the by-product, and in the real cell it also burns away the carbon anodes to make carbon dioxide. This is a good example of a case where the by-product has little commercial use, so the waste is real.

bullets: **Addition reactions** combine two molecules into one, so no atoms are wasted.
Ethene + steam → ethanol: Mr 28 + 18 = **46** and ethanol = **46**, so **100%**.
Haber process N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 has 100% atom economy, but a low yield per pass because it is reversible.
A high atom economy does **not** guarantee a high percentage yield.
Only reactions that make **one product** can be 100% atom economical.
Combustion of a fuel produces CO2 and H2O, both of which are products you might not want, so it depends on the desired product.
core.p: Some reactions have only one product, so all the atoms of the reactants are in the product. The best examples are **addition reactions**, such as ethene reacting with steam to make ethanol: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. The Mr values are 28 + 18 = 46, and the Mr of ethanol is 46, so the atom economy is 46 ÷ 46 × 100 = 100%. Hydrogenation of alkenes and the Haber process also have only one product, though the Haber process has a low percentage yield per pass.

bullets: Hydration: Mr C2H4 = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) = **28**; Mr H2O = **18**; total reactants = **46**.
Desired product: 2C2H5OH = 2 x 46 = **92**, so atom economy = 92 / 180 x 100 = **51.1%**.
By-product: 2CO2 = 2 x 44 = **88**, and 92 + 88 = 180, which checks conservation of mass.
Fermentation uses renewable sugar but has a **lower atom economy**; hydration has a higher atom economy but uses a **finite resource** (crude oil).
The **addition reaction** has 100% atom economy because there is only one product.
core.h: Worked reaction type 4: fermentation and hydration of ethene
core.p: Ethanol can be made by two different routes, and comparing them is a classic use of atom economy. In the hydration of ethene, C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, the only product is ethanol, so every reactant atom ends up in the desired product and the atom economy is 100%. In fermentation, C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2, the glucose splits into two ethanol molecules plus two carbon dioxide molecules, so some of the mass is lost as the by-product. The comparison shows how the atom economy depends on the equation chosen, not on how carefully the experiment is carried out.

bullets: Uses fewer **raw materials**, so conserves finite resources.
Produces less **waste**, so lower disposal costs and less pollution.
Lowers costs because less starting material is bought per unit of product, increasing **profit**.
Supports **sustainable development** and the principles of green chemistry.
Waste by-products may be hazardous or need expensive treatment.
Answer phrase: **'less waste is produced, so fewer raw materials are needed and it is more sustainable'**.
core.h: Why a high atom economy matters
core.p: Using a reaction with a high atom economy is more **sustainable** and usually more **profitable**. Fewer raw materials are needed for each tonne of product, so finite resources last longer. There is less waste to store, treat or dispose of, which is costly and can pollute the environment. Companies are also under pressure from regulations and public opinion to reduce waste. High atom economy therefore supports sustainable development, which means meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

bullets: **Atom economy** is calculated from the **balanced equation**; **percentage yield** is calculated from **experimental results**.
Atom economy shows the **waste built into the reaction**; yield shows the **waste from losses and incomplete reactions**.
A reaction with 100% yield may still waste a lot of reactant as by-products (low atom economy).
A reaction with 100% atom economy may still have a low yield (for example the reversible Haber process).
Both are used to judge how **efficient and sustainable** a process is.
Examiners may give a table of values and ask which process is better; consider both numbers.
core.h: Atom economy compared with percentage yield
core.p: These two ideas are often confused. **Percentage yield** looks at what actually happens in the experiment: it compares the real amount of product with the maximum amount. **Atom economy** looks at the equation: it tells you what proportion of the reactant mass could ever become the wanted product, even if the reaction worked perfectly. A reaction can have a very high percentage yield but a low atom economy if it makes a lot of by-product, and the other way round. A good industrial process needs both to be high.

bullets: **Atom economy**: the higher the better for less waste.
**Percentage yield**: a higher yield gives more product from the same reactants.
**Rate of reaction**: a fast reaction makes more product in a given time.
**Equilibrium position**: a reversible reaction may need special conditions to give a good yield.
**Energy costs and hazards**: high temperature or pressure costs more and may be dangerous.
**Useful by-products**: if a by-product can be sold (or recycled), the effective waste is lower.
core.p: The spec asks you to use atom economy and other factors to explain why a particular pathway is chosen. A company compares possible routes to a product. It looks at atom economy, percentage yield, the rate of reaction, whether the reaction is reversible and where equilibrium lies, the temperature and pressure needed (energy cost), how expensive or hazardous the raw materials are, and whether the by-products can be sold. The best route is usually a compromise.

bullets: A **useful by-product** can be sold, which makes the process more economical.
By-products can be **recycled** or used as a raw material in another process.
A **harmful by-product** needs treatment before disposal, adding cost.
Gaseous by-products such as CO2 add to greenhouse gas emissions if released.
Industrial sites often share by-products between neighbouring plants.
Answer phrase: **'the by-product can be sold so there is less waste'**.
core.p: If a reaction cannot avoid by-products, the waste can be reduced by finding a use for them. Chemical plants are designed so that the waste from one process becomes the raw material for another. For example, hydrogen from reforming and chlorine from electrolysis of brine are sold or used on the same site. If a by-product has a market, the real environmental and economic penalty of a low atom economy is smaller, which is why examiners sometimes ask whether a by-product is useful.

bullets: Write the Mr **under each substance** in the balanced equation.
**Multiply by coefficients** before adding.
Check **total reactants Mr = total products Mr**.
Do not round the Mr values; round only the final percentage.
If the question gives masses in kg or tonnes, the atom economy ratio still stays the same.
A final answer above 100% shows an error, such as using the wrong product on the top line.
core.h: Using large numbers and checking calculations
core.p: Examination questions can have equations with big molecules or large coefficients, so a tidy layout matters. Write the Mr of each formula under it in the equation, multiply by the coefficient, and keep a running total. Check by adding up the products: they must equal the reactants. If your two totals do not match, the equation is not balanced or an Mr has been miscalculated. Rounding should only be done at the end, to 3 significant figures or as the question demands.

bullets: **Relative formula mass and balanced equations**: needed for every calculation.
**Conservation of mass**: shows that all the mass of reactants is in the products, whether wanted or not.
**Percentage yield**: the paired idea in the same part of the spec.
**Extraction of metals and industrial processes**: examples with high and low atom economy.
**Using resources and sustainability**: reasons to reduce waste and conserve resources.
**Alkenes and addition reactions** (organic chemistry): 100% atom economy examples.
core.p: Atom economy brings together balanced equations, relative formula mass, conservation of mass and sustainability. It is directly paired with **percentage yield** in the same spec section, appears in the **extraction of metals** and **industrial processes** (Haber, contact process, electrolysis), and links to the **life cycle assessment** and **using resources** topics in the Chemistry of the atmosphere and Using resources units. It also helps explain why recycling is encouraged compared with extracting new materials.

exam: **'Calculate the atom economy'** is typically 2 to 3 marks: one for the correct Mr values, one for the correct fraction (desired ÷ total reactants), one for the final percentage.
Always write the equation **atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all reactants × 100** before substituting.
Remember to use the **balanced** equation and multiply by the coefficients; this is the most common lost mark.
**'Explain why a high atom economy is important'** (2 marks): less waste / fewer raw materials used (1), and better for the environment / more sustainable or lower costs (1).
**'Suggest why a company might choose reaction B instead of reaction A'**: compare atom economy, percentage yield, rate, cost, energy and the usefulness of by-products.
For comparison questions quote numbers from the data, for example 'A has an atom economy of 100% compared to 56%'.
If asked about a by-product, say whether it can be **sold or reused** to reduce waste.
A 6-mark question may combine calculation of atom economy and percentage yield: do each calculation separately and label your answers clearly.
Check the total Mr of reactants equals the total Mr of products; this is a quick way to catch mistakes.
Do not confuse **reaction pathway** factors: atom economy (equation), yield (practice), rate (speed), equilibrium (reversibility), cost and hazards.
Show the working even if you use a calculator, as method marks are available when the final answer is wrong.

mistakes.r: Only the desired product goes on the top; the bottom line is the sum of all reactants.
mistakes.w: Using the Mr of all products on the top line of the atom economy fraction.

mistakes.r: Use the coefficients: for example 3CO is 3 × 28 = 84, and 4Al is 4 × 27 = 108.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply Mr values by the big numbers in the balanced equation.

mistakes.r: Balance the equation first, because the atom economy depends on the ratio of moles.
Atom economy is from the equation and shows built-in waste; percentage yield is from experimental masses.
mistakes.w: Confusing atom economy with percentage yield.

mistakes.r: They are independent; a reaction can have 100% atom economy but a low yield if it is reversible.
mistakes.w: Saying that a high atom economy means a high yield.

mistakes.r: Say 'less waste is produced, so fewer raw materials are needed and it is more sustainable and cost-effective'.
mistakes.w: Writing 'less atoms are used' as the benefit of a high atom economy.

mistakes.r: Include every reactant shown in the equation, including gases like oxygen or carbon monoxide.
mistakes.w: Adding up only one of the reactants.

mistakes.r: By-products are real substances; mass is conserved, so the atoms end up in the by-products.
mistakes.w: Stating that waste products are 'lost' or 'disappear'.

mistakes.r: Keep Ar values as given and only round the final answer, to 3 s.f. or as asked.

summary: AQA expects you to calculate the **atom economy** of a reaction from its balanced equation and to explain why a high atom economy matters for sustainability and cost. You must also be able to use atom economy, percentage yield, rate and other factors to decide which reaction pathway to use to make a product.

terms.d: A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products.
The useful product that the reaction is intended to make.
A substance made in a reaction in addition to the desired product.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms shown in the formula.
The average mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
An equation with the same number of each type of atom on both sides, showing the ratio of moles of reactants and products.
The big number in front of a formula in an equation, showing how many moles of that substance react or form.
No atoms are lost or made in a chemical reaction, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
The actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
A reaction in which two molecules combine to form a single product, such as an alkene reacting with steam.
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
A resource that is used up faster than it is made, so it will eventually run out.
A reaction in which a substance is broken down into simpler substances by heating.
The loss of oxygen from a compound (in this context, metal oxide to metal).
The route, or series of reactions, used to make a particular product.
A reaction in which yeast turns glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide; its atom economy for ethanol is 51.1%.
The addition of steam to ethene to make ethanol, with a single product and so an atom economy of 100%.

worked.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. Calculate the atom economy for making calcium oxide. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16) (3 marks)
Iron is extracted in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Calculate the atom economy for making iron. (Ar: Fe = 56, C = 12, O = 16) (3 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: Reaction 1 has only one product so atom economy is 100% (1); fermentation makes CO2 as a by-product so atom economy is 51.1% (1); high atom economy means less waste / fewer raw materials used, which is more sustainable (1).
worked.q: Ethanol can be made from ethene and steam (C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH) or by fermentation (C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2). Explain why the first reaction has a higher atom economy and why this matters. (3 marks)
steps: Ethene + steam makes ethanol as the only product, so all the atoms in the reactants end up in the product.
This means the atom economy is 100%, whereas fermentation also makes carbon dioxide as a by-product, so its atom economy is lower (Mr: 2 × 46 = 92 out of 180, so 51.1%).
A higher atom economy means less waste and fewer raw materials are used, so the process is more sustainable and cheaper.
